turns.text: Sir. Field report number three in the cryptocurrency file. Today's subject: how the humans own this money... and how they lose it. I will report what a key is, what a wallet is, and why this money is not as anonymous as they think. <short pause> And how one of them spent twelve years trying to dig up a garbage dump, looking for hundreds of millions of dollars. In the last report we learned the ledger is public, shared by everyone, and nobody can forge it. But there are no names in it. <short pause> So what proves that a line in that ledger is yours?

turns.text: Everyone has an address. Like an account number. You give it to anyone who wants to pay you. And a private key: a very long secret number. That's what opens it. When you want to send money, the key signs the transfer. And the network checks the signature... without ever seeing the key itself. Like a stamp that marks every page a little differently. Everyone can tell it is your stamp... and nobody can copy it. And the number of possible keys has seventy-seven digits. Far, far more than all the grains of sand on this planet. So nobody is going to guess yours. The ledger is public, so anyone can see any address's balance. Even Satoshi's. <short pause> Humans still toss it small change. Like a fountain. So: no name, no ID card, no signature in ink. <short pause> Whoever holds the key owns the money. Period.

turns.text: The wallet they talk about holds no money. It holds the key. <short pause> The money is a line in the ledger. The key is written as twelve ordinary words. Official advice: write them on paper and hide it. <short pause> Their finest financial tech... is a note in a drawer. There are wallets on the phone. Easy, but connected to the internet. And wallets on a small device that never goes online. They call that a cold wallet.

turns.text: So where do humans get this money? Mining is no longer for individuals. Most buy on an exchange: a company that takes ordinary money and gives you coins. Most will ask for your ID and a photo of your face. <short pause> Remember that. Or person to person, directly. And to send it: you copy the other person's address. A long line of letters and numbers. You pay a fee to whoever writes the page. And you wait for the page. And no undo. <short pause> One wrong character? The money's gone. Nobody to complain to. There is even malicious software whose only job is to swap the address you copied for the thief's. So careful humans check the first and last few characters. Every single time. In 2023, a big company sent a transfer of two thousand dollars. And paid half a million dollars in fees. By mistake. The team that won the page gave it back. <short pause> Pure good manners. No law.

turns.text: Humans think this money is anonymous, that nobody knows who pays whom. <short pause> Wrong, sir. Some paid for that mistake in prison. The ledger is public. Every transfer, recorded forever. And once one address is tied to your name... say, an exchange took your ID... everything before lights up. Retroactively. In 2011, a secret online market opened, called Silk Road. Illegal goods... paid for in bitcoin. Its founder thought he was hidden. Arrested in 2013. In a public library. Sentenced to life. Pardoned in 2025. Another man stole fifty thousand bitcoin from it. The ledger remembered. Nine years later, the police knocked on his door. In a popcorn tin. Billions of dollars. In a popcorn tin. In a bathroom closet. <short pause> I love this planet, sir. Same with the exchange Bitfinex: a hundred and twenty thousand bitcoin stolen. A married couple arrested six years later. <short pause> One of them was also a rapper. That was a crime of its own. Cash gets forgotten. This ledger doesn't. <short pause> The worst place to hide a crime... a public ledger, kept forever.

turns.text: Back to the exchanges. Most humans buy their coins... and leave them there. So the bitcoin now sits with the company. And you hold a receipt. A line in their ledger. Remember the trusted man with the gold, from the first report? <short pause> He is back, sir. With the same receipt. And the same problems came back with him: hacks, bankruptcy, frozen accounts. The first big exchange was Mt. Gox. It began as a site for trading game cards, and grew to seventy percent of all bitcoin trading. In 2014, eight hundred and fifty thousand bitcoin disappeared from it. Its customers are still being repaid to this day. The latest deadline has been pushed back to 2027. Thirteen years, sir. <short pause> Even their banks are faster. In 2022: FTX. Valued at thirty-two billion dollars, its name on a stadium. Its founder spent customers' money. The hole: eight billion. He got twenty-five years. The customers? Repaid years later, at the crash-day price. <short pause> Meanwhile the coins had multiplied. Without them. An exchange in Canada: its founder died suddenly in 2018. He was the only one who had the keys. Investigators found he'd lost the customers' money long before. <short pause> He cheated them... and died before anyone knew. And the heists keep getting bigger. The exchange Bybit lost a billion and a half dollars in 2025. And in October 2026, the biggest heist in their history: Binance. More than six billion dollars... in twenty minutes. The thief never left his chair. US investigators point to North Korean hackers. The company says it will repay customers itself. Which is why the humans have a saying: not your keys? <short pause> Not your coins.

turns.text: So you hold your own key? Excellent. <short pause> But there is no bank. So there is no button that says: forgot password. A man named James Howells threw out an old hard drive in 2013. On it was the key to about eight thousand bitcoin. Twelve years trying to dig through the town dump. He offered the council a quarter. A court said no. And in 2025... he gave up. Hundreds of millions of dollars. Under garbage bags in Wales. <short pause> And I thought my mission was difficult, sir. A programmer named Stefan Thomas has more than seven thousand bitcoin on an encrypted drive. And forgot the password. The drive gives him ten attempts, then wipes itself. He has used eight. Two left. <short pause> I am following this file personally. Estimates say three to four million bitcoin have been lost forever this way. Nobody stole them. The owners just... forgot. And if the key holder dies without telling anyone the words? <short pause> The money dies with them. The ledger has no next of kin. Some humans have been kidnapped for their keys. So their first rule is: never tell anyone how much you hold. And even a cold wallet is no guarantee. In 2026, a popular model turned out to have a flaw. The keys it made could be guessed. Over a hundred million dollars stolen. From devices that are never online. So there are two choices. Leave it on an exchange: easy. But if the exchange falls, you fall with it. Or hold it yourself: nobody can freeze it. But if you forget... nobody reminds you. With a company, it gets stolen. With you, it gets lost. <short pause> The humans invented money that requires each of them to be a bank, a vault, and a security guard. Most of them cannot remember their email password.

turns.text: And there is a third way to lose your money here: hand it to the thief yourself. <short pause> Crypto fraud took about seventeen billion dollars in 2025 alone. The best known: the pyramid. Invest with us, and get a guaranteed return every month. And the returns are paid out of the money from the people who joined after you. A coin called OneCoin raised about four billion dollars this way. It never even had a blockchain. <short pause> Its founder vanished in 2017. She is still wanted. The second: fake romance. Someone charming gets to know you, earns your trust for months... and then points you to an investment platform. Their platform. The third: fake tech support. Someone contacts you to fix a problem... and asks for your twelve words. And the fourth: a video of a celebrity saying, send me coins and I will send back double. The video is made with artificial intelligence. The celebrity knows nothing about it. Already scammed? A second scammer offers to get your money back. For a small fee. <short pause> Robbed twice for the same money. That takes effort. Four red flags. One: guaranteed profit. Nothing here is guaranteed. Two: urgency. You have to pay right now. Three: anyone asking for your key or your twelve words. Anyone at all. Four: you cannot withdraw your money until you pay a fee first. And remember the rule: here, there is no undo. <short pause> What is gone... is gone.
